Vacuole. These are large, membrane-bound compartments found in plant and fungal cells that store water, nutrients, ions, pigments, and waste products. The central vacuole of plant cells can occupy up to ninety percent of the cell's total volume. It maintains turgor pressure—the outward pressure that keeps plants rigid and structured—while also providing the osmotic environment where cellular functions occur. Vacuoles perform digestive and storage roles similar to lysosomes in animal cells, though plant vacuoles are vastly larger.

The central vacuole is surrounded by a selective membrane called the tonoplast. This membrane regulates which ions and molecules can enter or leave the vacuole. The turgor pressure generated by the osmotic influx of water into the vacuole is what maintains cell rigidity and plant structure. This is why plants without adequate water become wilted—they lose turgor as water leaves the vacuole.

Vacuoles accumulate amino acids, sugars, ions, and proteins for storage and later use. They store pigments like anthocyanins and other compounds that give flowers and fruits their colors. They also sequester toxic secondary metabolites and oxidative byproducts—waste products that would be harmful if they remained in the cytoplasm. During plant growth, vacuolar expansion accounts for most of the rapid cell enlargement that follows cell division.

In times of environmental stress, particularly drought or salt exposure, the vacuole plays a crucial role in osmoregulation, helping plants survive adverse conditions. However, maintaining turgor demands continuous energy investment in ion pumps, making the vacuole a major cost of plant cell maintenance. Animal cells do have vacuoles, but they're smaller and rarer, used mainly for contracting to osmoregulate or for digesting intracellular material.
